name: Learn: CNI & Cluster Networking
objective: CKA › Services & Networking + Troubleshooting. Drill the whole pod-networking surface harder than the exam: how the CNI hands out pod IPs from the pod CIDR, the node-level CNI config, a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for a broken CNI, CoreDNS resolution, ClusterIP + endpoints, the full pod→Service datapath, headless Services, and NodePort. Graded exactly, per requirement.
description: Eight strict networking practicals on a real kind cluster. Each Check shows which requirements you met and the exact reason for any you missed.

questions.title: The CNI hands out pod IPs from the pod CIDR
questions.teach:
Kubernetes doesn't wire pod networking itself — a **CNI plugin** does. The kubelet calls it to attach each pod and lease it an IP out of the cluster **pod CIDR** (here `10.244.0.0/16`). See it with `kubectl get pod -o wide`.

**Gotcha:** no / broken CNI means no IP, so the pod is stuck `Pending`/`ContainerCreating` — never `Running`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cni-learn`, run a pod named `netcheck` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`).

Target: `netcheck` is `Running` with a `.status.podIP` inside the pod CIDR `10.244.0.0/16`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`, then `kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide` — the IP should start with `10.244.`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide

verification.description: netcheck is Running with a pod-CIDR IP (10.244.0.0/16)

questions.title: The CNI config lives on the node
questions.teach:
Each node carries its CNI config under `/etc/cni/net.d/`; the kubelet reads the first `*.conflist` there to know which plugin to call. On a kind node that file is `10-kindnet.conflist`, written by the kindnet DaemonSet. Each node also owns a slice of the pod CIDR in `.spec.podCIDR`.

**Gotcha:** the kubelet picks files in lexical order — a stray `00-*.conf` would shadow the real one.
questions.prompt:
No cluster change is needed here — this step inspects node `$W1`. It passes once node `$W1` has a `.spec.podCIDR` inside `10.244.0.0/16` AND the file `/etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist` exists on that node.

Target: `$W1` has a podCIDR and its kindnet CNI conflist is present.
questions.hint: `kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'` shows the node's slice; `docker exec $W1 ls /etc/cni/net.d` lists the CNI config. Both already hold on a healthy node.
questions.solution:
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'; echo
docker exec $W1 ls -l /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist

verification.description: $W1 has a podCIDR in 10.244.0.0/16 and /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist exists on the node

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a node with no CNI config
questions.teach:
When a node's CNI config under `/etc/cni/net.d/` is gone, the kubelet can't attach new pods there and they hang with no IP. The kindnet DaemonSet **rewrites that config every time its pod starts**, so bouncing kindnet on the bad node restores it.

**Gotcha:** target just the broken node with `--field-selector spec.nodeName=$W2` — don't delete the whole DaemonSet.
questions.prompt:
Pod `netbroken` (pinned to node `$W2`) is stuck with no IP — new pods on `$W2` aren't getting networking. Diagnose the fault on `$W2` and repair it so `netbroken` gets an IP. Don't delete `netbroken`; fix the node.

Target: `netbroken` has a `.status.podIP`.
questions.hint: Compare `$W2` to a healthy node: `docker exec $W2 ls /etc/cni/net.d` — the kindnet conflist is missing. Make kindnet rewrite it by restarting its pod on that node: `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l app=kindnet --field-selector spec.nodeName=$W2`. Wait ~15s.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W2 ls /etc/cni/net.d   # empty: the CNI config is gone
kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l app=kindnet --field-selector spec.nodeName=$W2
# the new kindnet pod rewrites /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist; netbroken then gets an IP
kubectl get pod netbroken -n cni-learn -o wide

verification.description: CNI restored on $W2 — netbroken now has an IP in the pod CIDR

questions.title: CoreDNS resolves Service names
questions.teach:
**CoreDNS** answers in-cluster DNS, resolving a Service's FQDN `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` to its clusterIP. Test from a pod with `nslookup <fqdn>`; a resolved `Address:` line means DNS works.

**Gotcha:** busybox `nslookup` is flaky with the `search` list — always query the **full FQDN**, not a short name, for a deterministic answer.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `dnscheck` (image `busybox:1.36`, `--restart=Never`) that resolves the API Service by its FQDN `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`.

Target: `dnscheck`'s logs show a resolved `Address` for that FQDN (no NXDOMAIN / 'can't resolve').
questions.hint: `kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`, then `kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn   # Address: 10.96.0.1

questions.title: Expose a Deployment (kube-proxy wires the endpoints)
questions.teach:
A **ClusterIP** Service gets a stable virtual IP that **kube-proxy** load-balances to the backing pods. `kubectl expose deployment <d> --port=80` creates it and copies the Deployment's selector, so its Endpoints auto-populate with the pod IPs.

**Gotcha:** zero endpoints almost always means the selector doesn't match the pod labels — check `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `web` (nginx, 3 replicas, label `app=web`) is already running in `cni-learn`. Expose it as a `ClusterIP` Service named `web` on port `80`.

Target: Service `web` is type ClusterIP, port 80, with 3 ready endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: `kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80`, then `kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn` (lists the pod IPs).
questions.solution:
kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80
kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn

verification.description: Service web: ClusterIP, port 80, 3 active endpoints

questions.title: Pod-to-pod through the Service
questions.teach:
This exercises the full datapath at once: DNS resolves `web.cni-learn` to the clusterIP, kube-proxy DNATs it to a backend pod, and the CNI carries the packet so nginx replies. Fetch it with `wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn`.

**Gotcha:** busybox `wget` needs `-qO-` to print to stdout — without it you get a downloaded file and empty logs.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `client` (image `busybox:1.36`, `--restart=Never`) that fetches `http://web.cni-learn` and prints the response.

Target: `client`'s logs show the nginx welcome page (it reached the Service).
questions.hint: `kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn`, then `kubectl logs client -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn
kubectl logs client -n cni-learn   # <title>Welcome to nginx!</title>

verification.description: client reached the web Service (full CNI + kube-proxy datapath)

questions.title: Headless Service returns pod IPs directly
questions.teach:
A **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`) gets no virtual IP and no kube-proxy load-balancing. Instead its DNS name resolves straight to the **individual pod IPs** (A records), which is how StatefulSets address peers.

**Gotcha:** `clusterIP: None` must be set at create time; you can't flip an existing ClusterIP Service to headless by editing.
questions.prompt:
Create a **headless** Service named `web-hl` in `cni-learn` selecting `app=web` on port `80` (set `clusterIP: None`). It targets the existing `web` pods.

Target: Service `web-hl` has `clusterIP: None`, selector `app=web`, port 80, and endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cni-learn create service clusterip web-hl --clusterip=None --tcp=80:80`, then add the selector: `kubectl -n cni-learn set selector svc web-hl 'app=web'` (or write YAML with `clusterIP: None`).
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-hl, namespace: cni-learn }
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
YAML
kubectl get endpoints web-hl -n cni-learn

verification.description: web-hl: clusterIP None, selector app=web, port 80, has endpoints

questions.title: NodePort opens the Service on every node
questions.teach:
A **NodePort** Service builds on ClusterIP and also opens a port (default range `30000–32767`) on **every** node; kube-proxy forwards `nodeIP:nodePort` to the backends. It's the simplest way to reach a Service from outside the cluster.

**Gotcha:** a nodePort outside 30000–32767 is rejected unless the apiserver's `--service-node-port-range` was widened.
questions.prompt:
Create a `NodePort` Service named `web-np` in `cni-learn` selecting `app=web`, service port `80`, pinned to nodePort `30080`.

Target: Service `web-np` is type NodePort with port 80, nodePort 30080, selector `app=web`, and endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: Write YAML with `type: NodePort` and `ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080}]`, selector `app=web`. (`kubectl expose` won't let you pin the nodePort.)
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-np, namespace: cni-learn }
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080 } ]
YAML
kubectl get svc web-np -n cni-learn

verification.description: web-np: NodePort, port 80, nodePort 30080, selector app=web, has endpoints
